title: Ali 'The Greatest' but Maguire the latest to win in Croke Park
description: With Katie Taylor set to be the first boxer to headline Croke Park since Muhammad Ali beat Al 'Blue' Lewis in 1972, BBC Sport NI catches up with Paddy Maguire, who was last to box on that iconic night.
fullText:
Croke Park's storied history contains some of Irish sport's most seminal moments.

Primarily a stadium for Gaelic games, there have been occasions when other sports graced the hallowed turf and on 19 July 1972, punches replaced points as Muhammad Ali took on Al 'Blue' Lewis.

When Katie Taylor makes her final career ringwalk on Saturday with the undisputed light-welterweight crown on offer against Flora Pili, 54 years will have passed since 'The Greatest' starred at the since redeveloped venue.

While Ali was the main attraction in 1972, it was Belfast's Paddy Maguire who boxed last on that balmy Wednesday evening, coming through on points against France's Guy Caudron.

"It's hard to believe it has taken so long for boxing to return to Croke Park," Maguire told BBC Sport NI.

As an amateur, Maguire won featherweight silver at the 1966 Commonwealth Games in Jamaica - a medal that was "hard won as they were all tough fights".

A switch to the professional code prompted another move, this time to London where he linked up with manager Paddy Byrne.

It was this relationship which ultimately led to Maguire and Pat McCormack earning a slot on Ali's undercard, which also featured Donegal's Paddy Doherty, plus future light-heavyweight world champion John Conteh and heavyweight Joe Bugner, who would twice lose to Ali in later years.

"Pat and myself were great friends and had the same manager, so it was great for us to be on such a huge bill," Maguire recalled.

"To be a man from the Kashmir Road in Belfast, fighting on Muhammad Ali's bill was great, but I could never understand why there were so few Irish fighters involved."

Aged 30, Ali - who had iconic wins against George Foreman and Joe Frazier to come in his career - accepted a reported £300,000 offer by Kerry promoter Michael 'Butty' Sugrue to fight in Ireland.

Battling a cold, Ali secured an 11th-round victory over Lewis and while just 17,000 made their way through the turnstiles - 15,000 short of the break-even mark -others were more creative in how they entered.

One of those attending by conventional means was Kilkenny hurling great Eddie Keher in a year in which he collected the fourth of his six All-Ireland senior medals.

A boxing fan, Keher recalls burning the midnight oil in his youth with his father, tuning into radio commentary of heavyweight greats Joe Louis, Rocky Marciano and then Ali.

With the promotional push for Croke Park in full swing, an idea was hatched to have the pair meet at the Kilternan Hotel - "a high point" in his life.

"I was dumbstruck when I saw him [Ali]. He was different from what I imagined because he wasn't the flamboyant guy we'd seen on television," Keher told BBC Sport NI's GAA Social podcast.

"The press were outside and I had two hurls and a sliotar [ball]. I was supposed to teach him how to play hurling, but he was finding it hard to hit the ball with two hands, so he was hitting it with one hand like a tennis racquet.

"He was still the ordinary guy but then he came up close to me and said, 'we'll put on a show for these guys' so he went to hit me with his hurl and I put up mine to save me. Then he was going around fencing with the hurl and became the Muhammad Ali we knew."

While Keher and those in attendance remember the occasion with fondness, behind the scenes things were a little more chaotic.

Fight gloves had not been sourced, prompting a last-minute scramble to have some sent from England, resulting in a late start to the undercard which would ultimately leave Maguire waiting until after the main event before he boxed.

"There weren't too many left by that stage, but I ended up on last as I was seen as an exciting, all-action pressure fighter," Maguire reasoned.

"Maybe their idea was to have me on last to try and keep people there."

Maguire remembers Ali as a "lovely man" - and it would not be the last time the boxers' paths would cross.

After British and Commonwealth bantamweight title defeats, Maguire would avenge a previous loss against David Needham in 1975 to get his hands on the Lonsdale Belt - and in the build-up, reunited with Ali at Wembley.

In August 1977, they met again in the Grosvenor House Hotel for a testimonial in honour of Ali's friend Paddy Monaghan, the Fermanagh-born bare-knuckle boxer.

"There were ups and down," Maguire says of his career, "but it's one I'm proud of."

While his days in the ring were over, he would remain connected to the sport, serving as a member of the British Boxing Board of Control's Northern Ireland Council.

On Saturday, Maguire will watch from home as Taylor, a trailblazer for women's boxing, makes the same walk as Ali.

"I've had the opportunity to tell my kids and grandchildren about my time there, so for those boxing this time, they can do the same one day," he said.

"Katie Taylor has had a great career and deserves her big night, but hopefully it's not another 50 years before boxing's back in Croke Park."

title: The transfers to watch before window closes
description: BBC Sport's football experts picks out the standout transfers that could go through before Tuesday's 23:00 BST English deadline.
fullText:
The summer transfer window may have been open since 15 June but several Premier League clubs are still scrambling to get key deals over the line before Tuesday's 23:00 BST deadline.

From Julian Alvarez and Enzo Fernandez to Cody Gakpo and Ismaila Sarr, some of football's biggest names could yet be on the move.

But they will have to battle the clock to earn their dream moves before the market closes.

With that in mind, BBC Sport's football reporters have picked out the high-profile moves which could go through during what promises to be a busy ending to the window.

Julian Alvarez's potential move to Arsenal could be the biggest deal to watch, with the Atletico Madrid striker's future now hanging in the balance.

The 26-year-old is caught between his desire to leave Atletico and the club's refusal to sell him to Barcelona. But they would do a deal with Arsenal.

The Gunners have had a long-term interest in Alvarez and have been monitoring the dramatic situation, with Atleti looking for a fee of 150m euros (£128m).

Alvarez has missed multiple training sessions and did not travel to face Sevilla on Saturday, with Simeone saying he wasn't well enough.

Simeone, meanwhile, has attempted to keep the door open, saying he will "do everything" he can to make Alvarez feel important when he returns to training.

Enzo Fernandez missed Sunday's Premier League win over Brighton and his future is under increasing uncertainty, having been linked with a big-money move to Manchester City.

Enzo Maresca worked with the Argentina midfielder at Chelsea and needs to bolster his ranks following the departures of Rodri, Bernardo Silva, Nico Gonzalez and Tijjani Reijnders this summer.

Any potential move would likely be a club record deal, surpassing the £116m paid for Elliot Anderson earlier this summer.

Fernandez potentially leaving for Manchester City could open the door for fellow midfielder Lamine Camara to arrive at Stamford Bridge from Monaco as his replacement.

It could be Chelsea's 13th deal coming in, with exits exceeding 30 players as the Blues are expected to surpass the Premier League player sales record they set at £300m last season.

There is further intrigue around departures with Mykhailo Mudryk looking for a loan move and still a lack of clarity on the futures of Pedro Neto and Tosin Adarabioyo. The likes of Dario Essugo, Deivid Washington and Shim Mheuka could also leave.

Manchester City have opened talks with Liverpool about signing attacker Cody Gakpo and the Netherlands international is open to the move.

But Liverpool would only be willing to sanction the transfer if they can bring in one more attacking player, in addition to Bradley Barcola.

Spurs are also interested but City are willing to offer a deal worth around £85m and sources indicate that City is Gakpo's preferred destination.

With Gakpo's future up in the air, Liverpool have turned their attentions to Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr after having two bids for Yankuba Minteh rejected by Brighton.

The Seagulls want more than the £60m offered by Liverpool and it remains to be seen whether Iraola's side go back in for him.

Like the Gambian, Sarr is a right-sided winger and the Reds initially enquired about the Senegal international last week, but that was rebuffed by Crystal Palace.

Tottenham are in advanced talks to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton, with Richarlison set to move in the opposite direction.

Although a deal for Ndiaye is largely agreed between the two clubs, it remains unclear whether he will make the switch to north London, with Manchester City among the clubs to have expressed an interest.

Everton are open to selling Ndiaye, 26, after he rejected multiple contract offers and held talks with Saudi club Al-Hilal earlier this summer.

Meanwhile, Everton have agreed terms in principle to re-sign striker Richarlison after he told Spurs head coach Roberto de Zerbi "too many times that he wants to leave".

Everton are growing increasingly confident of completing a loan deal to bring Jack Grealish back from Manchester City, although the precise terms of any agreement remain complicated as the England international enters the final year of his contract at Etihad Stadium.

Grealish has prioritised a return to Everton, where he spent last season on loan, over the option of rejoining his boyhood club Aston Villa, who have also expressed an interest.

Just a few hours after the unveiling of Nico Gonzalez, Matthias Jaissle made it clear he would continue to push for further deals in the final throes of the window.

Another forward is on the German's wishlist and Newcastle have a longstanding interest in Lille's Matias Fernandez-Pardo, whose creativity and ability to play in a number of positions across the frontline is a huge draw. The 21-year-old also fits the age range Newcastle have targeted this summer.

This would be a complicated deal to do in the final days of the window, but it was a little telling that Lille manager Davide Ancelotti left Fernandez-Pardo out of his squad for the weekend's game against Paris St-Germain and has decided to exclude him from training until the window shuts.

Unless there is a very late, and unexpected, development around Marcus Rashford, it feels as if Manchester United's deadline-day business will centre around Joshua Zirkzee and the smaller deals they can do.

Fiorentina wanted to take the Netherlands forward on loan, with an option to buy.

United, ideally, would prefer to sell, or at least get a loan with an obligation.

With no agreement possible, Fiorentina are now looking elsewhere.

However, Juventus are keen on Zirkzee, although a move for the 25-year-old hinges on Canada forward Jonathan David leaving for Atletico Madrid.

Zirkzee's exit might open the door for a left-back or a reinforcement in the forward department, although that too might initially be a loan.

title: Barcola - the 'grasshopper' who has overcome setbacks
description: As Liverpool agree a £123m deal for Bradley Barcola, BBC Sport looks at how he has ridden triumphs and setbacks to reach the top with the help of his family.
fullText:
There was a moment, not so long ago, when Bradley Barcola's career appeared to have stalled.

Having earned rave reviews after nailing down a regular starting place in Lyon's starting XI under Peter Bosz, the 20-year-old winger was out of favour and in the reserves by the time the Dutch coach was replaced by Laurent Blanc in October 2022.

According to L'Equipe,, external Barcola was close to joining Swiss club St Gallen in January 2023 in order to get more game time before an act of petulance by a team-mate helped pave his return to the side.

Fans were unhappy with the team's poor form - making first-choice forward Karl Toko Ekambi a target for their frustrations.

The relationship between the Cameroon international and Lyon's ultras fractured further when he stormed down the tunnel and kicked a rubbish bin in frustration after being substituted during a 2-1 home defeat by Strasbourg.

The incident was caught on camera and Toko Ekambi never played for Lyon again.

That presented Barcola with an opportunity which he seized. He started the majority of the remaining matches that season, scoring five times, including a winner at champions-in-waiting Paris St-Germain in April 2023.

Five months after that goal at the Parc des Princes, Barcola was a PSG player.

His reported £38.5m move - two weeks after Brazil forward Neymar swapped Paris for Saudi Arabia - came with Lyon struggling in the table and also unable to sign replacements because of financial restrictions.

"Barcola's first game for PSG was back at Lyon," Pierre-Etienne Minonzio, football journalist for L'Equipe, told BBC Sport.

"He was booed by the Lyon fans because it was just after the transfer. PSG boss Luis Enrique asked Barcola, who was very young at the time, if he was ready to play.

"He said yes, came on as a substitute, and it was impressive."

Barcola, nicknamed the 'grasshopper' because of his speed, agility and slight frame, has since gone on to win three Ligue 1 titles and back-to-back Champions Leagues in his three seasons in the French capital. He broke into the France side two years ago, and scored three times as this summer's World Cup as they reached the semi-finals.

With Liverpool agreeing a £123m deal to sign him, Barcola is on his way to the Premier League.

It has been quite the journey from kicking a ball about as a schoolboy on the playing fields of Vaulx-en-Velin - situated to the east of Lyon - to becoming a superstar worth nine figures. But the path has not been without challenges.

"Barcola is hugely ambitious," added Minonzio.

"He is from a generation of young French talent who are prepared to work hard and want to be a better version of themselves.

"They will do whatever they have to do to get there. They don't ask questions - they just do it."

Why Liverpool are ready to make Barcola third £100m signing

Luis Enrique quiet on Barcola future

Barcola's family have been with him on every step of his journey, from starting out as the shy boy who played for his local team AS Buers Villeurbanne to joining Lyon's academy at the age of eight, to making his Lyon debut 11 years later, to becoming a double Champions League winner with PSG in Budapest in May.

Born Bradley Jean-Manuel Essolisam Addo Barcola on 2 September 2002, he has five siblings - including one other footballer, his older brother Malcolm, 27, a goalkeeper for Ittihad Tanger in Morocco and the Togo national team.

It was their mother who encouraged them to take up football - she would attend their matches and film the brothers playing.

"It's rare but she's the one who gave us passion [for the sport]," Barcola, who looked up to Cristiano Ronaldo and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang, said in an interview with Uefa in 2024.

His father, Yves, had a passion for sport and a strong work ethic, and would gather them in the family living room to watch clips of their matches back together.

Malcolm has spoken about growing up with his younger brother.

"Every weekend, we went to the local stadium," he told newspaper Le Progres., external "My father made Bradley do specific work in front of goal, and me, as a goalkeeper... he made me work too. We complemented each other well."

Long before Barcola, graduates from Lyon's academy included Karim Benzema, who has won multiple Champions Leagues with Real Madrid and the Ballon d'Or, Arsenal FA Cup winner Alexandre Lacazette, and France 2018 World Cup winners Samuel Umtiti and Corentin Tolisso.

More recent graduates include Manchester City forward Rayan Cherki and Chelsea full-back Malo Gusto.

Aged 17, Barcola scored 11 goals in 17 league matches for Lyon's Under-19 team before signing his first professional contract two years later in 2021.

It was a huge moment for the Barcola family.

During his rise to fame and fortune, Barcola has spoken about the importance of his family in keeping him grounded.

When the player was roundly criticised for missing chances against Newcastle in the Champions League in his first season at PSG, he turned to his family for support.

"My parents and I talk about everything," Barcola said in an interview with French newspaper Le Parisien. "As soon as something goes wrong, on or off the pitch, we talk about it. I've got my older brother, too.

"When things aren't going so well, I need to see them and get their advice.

"When they tell me 'you're messing up', it's because they're right. And when they tell me I've played well, it's because I have. I don't listen to what's said outside."

Asked about his son's reaction to the criticism following the Newcastle match, Yves Barcola said: "We talked to him about it, it's the kind of thing that doesn't affect him. That's what he tells us, it pushes him to do more.

"He's never been given anything in his young career, he's always had to earn things with his patience and qualities."

Paris St-Germain boss Luis Enrique has described Barcola as a "balanced person, very sensible, humble, hard-working, with great family values".

"After Newcastle at the Parc, he was very criticised, unfairly, and that did not reflect reality," added Luis Enrique. "He was able to calmly manage the difficult moments post-Newcastle in the best possible way."

What strengths might Barcola bring to Anfield?

'Liverpool have to get Barcola deal done'

Barcola is the statement signing Liverpool fans have craved all summer.

With his expensive price tag, however, comes pressure.

He will be expected to hit the ground running, but he does have form against Premier League opposition.

Barcola has come up against numerous English clubs during his time at PSG. He scored in a 4-2 Champions League win over Manchester City in January 2025 before finding the net in each leg against Chelsea in the last-16 last season.

Liverpool and their new boss Andoni Iraola will take positives that Barcola settled so quickly after his high-profile move to PSG.

"He went to Paris St-Germain for something like 50m euros, which was a huge amount considering he had only played something like one full season in Ligue 1," said Minonzio.

"It was an insane amount of money for someone who had not really done anything, but Luis Enrique saw something in him.

"Luis Enrique said: 'Whatever it costs, we need him because he has huge potential.'

"Full credit to Luis Enrique because he saw things a lot of people didn't see.

"Barcola started well at PSG but after some months he had some issues because opposition defenders noticed that he was always doing the same kind of dribble.

"He was aware of that and he managed to change and have a wider range of tricks.

"He has a lot more qualities than two or three years ago."

Minonzio added: "Personally I think Liverpool is a good fit for Barcola, especially because of Iraola. He is so good at improving players and Barcola is not the finished product.

"Sometimes he runs and runs and runs, and then his finishing is not always good. He has to improve and I think he will.

"It was exactly the same with Ousmane Dembele. Two or three years ago, Dembele was so good at dribbling and running, but sometimes when he was in front of goal he was making bad choices.

"Barcola is a bit like that in the finishing aspect of his game, but he will improve with the right manager - and I think Iraola is the right manager."

Sylvain Ripoll was Barcola's France Under-21 coach in 2023.

"He's very endearing, always in a good mood," he said of Liverpool's new signing.

"He might seem a little reserved, but he has character on the pitch and in his decision-making. He brings something different to the table, all with an exceptional mindset."

Luis Enrique has gone on record as saying signing Barcola in 2023 was a "gamble".

title: Martinez is eighth Chelsea-Villa deal in four years
description: After Emiliano Martinez's move, BBC Sport looks at why Aston Villa and Chelsea have become one of the Premier League’s busiest transfer partnerships since 2022.
fullText:
Chelsea have signed Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez from Aston Villa for £7.5m - the eighth deal between the two clubs in the past four years.

The 33-year-old, who won the World Cup in 2022, has moved to Stamford Bridge on a three-year deal.

Former Arsenal goalkeeper Martinez joined Villa in 2020 and made 256 appearances, helping the club win the Europa League last season.

"I'm delighted to be at this football club," Martinez said.

"Coming to Chelsea, for me and my family, was an easy decision to make and I'm just over the moon - I can't wait to get started.

'I want to be successful here. I'm someone who wants to win at everything I do and I want to bring that here to this football club because it's a football club that wins titles, so I think it's a good match."

Martinez's move to Chelsea comes after Nicolas Jackson's transfer the other way last week.

No two Premier League clubs have exchanged more players, on permanent or loan deals, in the past four years.

The relationship began after Chelsea's owners, BlueCo, took control of the club in 2022 and signed Carney Chukwuemeka from Villa for £20m that summer. Ian Maatsen (£37.5m, to Villa), Omari Kellyman (£19m, to Chelsea) and Axel Disasi (a £5m loan deal, to Villa) subsequently moved between the clubs.

This summer alone has brought four more deals. Morgan Rogers completed a £117m move Chelsea, while Alejandro Garnacho joined Villa on loan with a conditional obligation to buy in a deal worth around £43m.

Jackson then moved to Villa for £65m, before Martinez followed.

Since 2022, Chelsea have paid Aston Villa £163.5m for players. Villa have spent £102.5m on Chelsea players including Axel Disasi's loan fee. That figure could rise to £150.5m should certain criteria be met to make Garnacho's loan move permanent. Chelsea believe the terms are easily reachable.

Chelsea and Villa have done business before. Tammy Abraham, Ross Barkley, Danny Drinkwater, Ryan Bertrand, Steve Sidwell and Andy Townsend are among those to have moved between the clubs during the Premier League era, while John Terry joined Villa after leaving Chelsea.

But the recent volume of business between the clubs has not gone unnoticed elsewhere in the Premier League, at a time when both have had to navigate domestic and European financial regulations. One source told BBC Sport that a number of club executives have raised questions about the frequency of the dealings.

There is no suggestion, though, that either club have broken any rules.

BBC Sport has approached Chelsea and Aston Villa for comment.

BBC Sport has counted every permanent transfer and loan between Premier League clubs since the summer of 2022, restricting the analysis to the 15 sides who have been in the top flight throughout that period.

There is a tie at the top: Chelsea have done eight deals with Villa, and another eight with Brighton.

Newcastle United and Nottingham Forest are next on six, followed by Arsenal and Chelsea on five.

Chelsea feature in six of the 10 busiest club pairings, illustrating the scale of their player trading since the BlueCo consortium completed its takeover.

BlueCo's £4.25bn purchase of Chelsea ended Roman Abramovich's 19-year ownership and ushered in a period of significant squad turnover.

But Villa's close relationship with Chelsea also has a more specific explanation.

Chelsea co-owner Behdad Eghbali and Villa owner Nassef Sawiris have developed a close working relationship and have communicated directly over transfer business.

That relationship has spanned several transfer windows and included Rogers' move to Stamford Bridge this summer.

Chelsea did not have a clear run at Rogers, though - as Arsenal also wanted to sign him, and it was the player's decision to move to Stamford Bridge.

Uefa has the power to scrutinise transfers completed between the same clubs within a 45-day period. Garnacho's move to Villa - on an initial loan deal - came two days after Rogers signed for Chelsea. Jackson's permanent transfer went through 38 days after the Rogers one.

But a timeline on its own is not evidence that the deals were in any way related.

Villa, for instance, could point to their long-held interest in Jackson, who previously worked with head coach Unai Emery at Villarreal.

Chelsea, meanwhile, could argue their interest in Martinez was independent of previous dealings with Villa and would have been pursued regardless of the club he played for. The goalkeeper had attracted interest from Juventus earlier in the window, with a finger injury understood to have scuppered a move.

There are broader reasons why domestic transfers remain attractive, but money is often the biggest factor.

Premier League clubs generally have greater spending power than most teams elsewhere in Europe, meaning another English side may be among the few buyers capable of meeting the fee and wage demands of a selling club.

That can make domestic deals particularly attractive when clubs are trying to move on high-value players. Signing from within the league also reduces some of the uncertainty, with recruitment teams already familiar with a player's qualities and performances.

Yet even in a league where domestic trading is commonplace, the frequency of deals between Villa and Chelsea stands out.

title: Are Charlton ready to challenge? - Sam Parkin's EFL takeaways
description: BBC Final Score pundit Sam Parkin looks at the weekend's talking points in the EFL, including a perfect start for Charlton Athletic.
fullText:
With most sides having completed their opening three matches of the new season, BBC Final Score pundit Sam Parkin gives his takeaways from across the EFL on some of the early high flyers and strugglers.

Charlton finished 19th in the Championship in 2025-2026 after coming up from League One the previous season, so does three successive wins suggest the Addicks are ready to 'kick-on'?

Parkin: "I'm sure if you offered Nathan Jones and the most ardent of supporters a mid-table finish now, they'd snap your hand off for it. So, I don't think anyone will be getting carried away.

"I think that first season is always about staying in the division, being defensively strong. The majority of their victories last season were by narrow margins - like today.

"I think they look a bit more attacking this season. He played a wing-back system before, and they they look like they're playing with wingers this season, which is a bit more attack-minded.

"When they got promoted, they signed a lot of good lads from League One to try and make the step up with them to the Championship. This summer I think there's been a slightly different tack there in terms of recruitment, with a lot more experience - like today's goalscorer Karlan Grant and Nathaniel Chalobah - coming to The Valley.

"There's definitely slight differences in the way that they're setting up, and the style".

Charlton maintain 100% start against lowly Preston

Swansea have had three successive mid-table finishes in the Championship, but Saturday's 3-0 win at Derby continued their flying start to 2025-2026 with seven points from three games so far:

Parkin: "Despite the manager (Victor Matos) being there last year, I think they were probably a little bit unknown coming into the season.

"They had a really interesting summer in terms of the players they signed, bringing in Celtic defender Stephen Welsh, and today's first scorer - Ghana winger Joseph Opoku - from Belgium.

"So, I think they're quite forward thinking in the way that they go about signing players, and and the one thing about Swansea is you that, give or take, you know the way they are going to play. It's always quite a stylish brand of football.

"I think they've had a terrific start, but I'm not sure they'll have the consistency to be challenging the higher echelons of the division, but now that the play-offs are extended to six teams, they could look to maybe make one of those positions.

"The other side of the coin is obviously Derby are winless and it was probably a good time to play Derby, with their injuries and the frustrations over the takeover not happening."

Burnley agreed to part company with former Championship-winning manager Scott Parker in the summer, and bring in former Genk boss Nicky Hayen - but they are yet to win in the league:

Parkin: "It's the case with all the relegated sides that you have to give them a little bit of time to acclimatize. I think that's natural. There might be some in the dressing room who don't see themselves as being second-tier footballers.

"That's the reality, and some may still move before the window closes, so we won't know exactly what squad he'll be working with. But my sentiment with them is that they've got brilliant individuals, whoever sticks around, and I'm sure they'll be able to add as well in both the windows.

"So they're going to be competitive in terms of the quality of players. It's just getting that cohesion, which may take a bit of time with a new manager.

"Probably in contrast to West Ham and Wolves who I think have both got real goal power, I'm not sure I'm seeing the same kind of power in that area of the pitch for Burnley.

"There's not a number of them that jump off the page that are going to guarantee a good return of goals. That would be my biggest question mark about them at the moment.

"But as hard as it'll be for supporters to hear, I don't think it's any shame losing at Norwich, because Norwich are going to be right up there in my opinion this season. That's probably a given considering how well they finished last season under Philippe Clement."

The Owls finally saw new ownership take over the club this summer after a long battle, and beat Bromley 7-2 in front of 30,000 fans at Hillsbrough:

Parkin: "Despite the pain of the past few years and the fans' uncertainty, they've got their club to go and support again, and albeit it's in the third tier, the attendances will be huge.

"They never wavered their support really under very, very difficult ownership to put it lightly across the past few years. So there's a new dawn there.

"The side played well against Bradford, certainly for 45 minutes in their maiden home game in the league this season, but just couldn't get the goal.

"So to get those early goals today in the first half will have given them the belief to go on. They've got some really exciting young players and, despite them being in League One, with the size of that club, people want to go and play for you.

"People will want to be on that journey. They'll want to play in front of a packed crowd every week, and the club name will sell itself.

"They're going to be strong. I thought it'd probably take a little bit of time, but that will do them wonders today getting such a handsome victory at home."

Salford City finished eighth in 2024-2025, and then lost the 2025-2026 League Two play-of final, before sacking Karl Robinson. His successor, Peter Cklamovski, has lost his opening three league matches:

Parkin: "If you were a fan, you'd have been really enthused again in the transfer window. Two names that jump out at me - Luke Molyneux, probably the best attacking player at Doncaster for a number of seasons, and striker Macaulay Langstaff from Millwall.

"He didn't have a great time at Millwall in terms of goals, but he's probably better than League Two. So to get those two over the line in the summer, naturally, you would have felt that, attacking wise, they were going to be very good - and it's not translated that way in the opening weeks of the season.

"It's early days, but the ownership will be scratching their heads a little bit, because the budget will be very competitive again and beaten play-off finalists last year, you'd expect them to be around it. So, really surprised.

"It'll get better for them, I'm sure, but when you take the Salford job, you're always under probably a bit more pressure than some of the jobs in League Two because of the resources and the magnitude of some of the names that are involved."

Sam Parkin was speaking to BBC Sport England's Tim Durrans

title: In-form quartet all win away to snap at heels of leaders Coleraine
description: BBC Sport NI explores the main talking point of the weekend from within the Irish Premiership.
fullText:
Who says it is too early to look at the Irish Premiership table?

It is, off course, too early to be talking about title races, European places and relegation battles but there has been plenty to ponder after a week four of the Irish Premiership which yielded a clean sweep of five away wins.

Currently, four teams sit on nine points after winning three games and losing one, the in-form quartet tucked in just one point behind early leaders Coleraine.

Dungannon Swifts, Carrick Rangers, Crusaders and Linfield all won their fixtures on Saturday to occupy second to fifth and have impressed so far.

But what have those four teams shown during the early weeks of this season? BBC Sport NI explores some of the talking points from within each club.

For Dungannon Swifts, the most obvious improvement has been the manner in which they have recovered from their opening day defeat.

Rodney McAree's side began the campaign with a 3-1 home loss against Coleraine, but have responded with victories over Portadown, Bangor and Cliftonville.

That represents a significant improvement on last season when the Swifts made a really concerning start to the campaign and lost their opening five league fixtures.

Dungannon have secured a top six finish for the past two seasons and manager Rodney McAree will want to repeat the feat this term.

Midfielder Sean McAllister has already stood out, scoring three goals so far and has been heavily involved when the Swifts push into the final third.

New signings such as Kris Lowe have also impressed with former Portadown boss Niall Currie saying the Swifts side is the "strongest" it has ever been, as they aim to seal another chance at European football.

"I look at Rodney McAree's squad now and, to me, this is the strongest Dungannon squad there has been," Currie said on Sportsound.

"Rodney has gone out and got strength and depth. Some of the players who are not even making the squad at the minute for the Swifts are a lot of players who would certainly have started a few years ago."

After last season's seventh-place finish and resultant play-off involvement, and with the team overflowing with Irish League experience, it is maybe no surprise that Carrick have made a strong start to the campaign.

Paul Heatley continues to be a threat in their attack and certainly does not perform like a player who had to be persuaded out of retirement by manager Stephen Baxter in the summer.

The 39-year-old, who signed a new one-year deal during the summer, has already netted three goals so far with his partnership with Danny Gibson continuing to give the opposition's defence headaches.

During their emphatic 4-0 win over Bangor, they were also denied by the woodwork four times with Seasiders manager Lee Feeney saying that his side "were lucky it was only four", showing the complete dominance that Carrick enjoyed.

It will be a big next few fixtures for Stephen Baxter's side, who face Linfield, Cliftonville Ballymena United, Larne and Glentoran in September.

After only securing their Premiership status last season through the promotion/relegation play-off and then losing their opening fixture against rivals Cliftonville, early alarm bells may have been starting to sound among Crusaders fans.

They have certainly stopped now, though, with the side showing their grit to earn a 2-1 win over Glentoran at the Oval and extend their winning sequence to three.

Following a dismal 2025-26 campaign, it was a challenging off season for Declan Caddell, who has had to rebuild his team following key player's exits such as Fraser Bryden and Musa Dibaga.

Caddell opted once again to explore the Scottish market during the transfer window and, so far, the new signings have impressed with Scots Owen Wardell and Aaron Reid scoring in east Belfast.

Last season, the Crues struggled due to relying on Bryden for goals but pressing on the counter-attack has emerged as one of the new tactics the side are using early this season.

"They have been good on the counter-attack. When they have done it, they have created opportunities," said Sean Ward after their win over Glentoran.

"Crusaders have relied on hitting on the counter which is a strategy I have no doubt they will use for much of the season.

"It has worked massively for them."

Few clubs will attract as much attention after an opening day defeat as Linfield did when they lost against Ballymena United, a result that immediately raised questions around how the side would respond.

However, after another professional display from the Blues which saw them breeze past Limavady, they have now won three games in a row and registered clean sheets in their past two matches.

At the Limavady Showgrounds, Adam Frizzell assisted Matthew Fitzptarick's opening goal of the season before scoring himself in the second half.

Questions still remain around the Linfield squad and its depth which will likely be tested as the season progresses, but the side have already shown the qualities needed to bounce back from disappointment.

The experienced David Healy will know more than most that the table will change constantly but he will also be aware that the opening weekends are far from irrelevant as the race for the Gibson Cup starts to heat up.

title: Slow start makes me want to stay - Norris extends McLaren deal to 2030
description: In an exclusive BBC Sport interview, Lando Norris explains why he has signed a new contract that will keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030.
fullText:
Lando Norris says signing a new contract that will keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030 was "quite an easy yes for me".

The world champion, whose new deal was announced on Saturday, said he "didn't even have a look" at other teams before deciding to commit his future to the team he has been with since his Formula 1 debut in 2019.

"There was some interest from elsewhere," Norris said in an interview with BBC Sport, "but I don't want to go anywhere. I don't want to be with another team. I don't want to spend time with other people.

"That's why it really was probably one of the easiest decisions I've made since being in Formula 1."

The Briton had no need to rush his decision to commit to McLaren because his existing contract still had more than a year to run.

But he says the idea "became a topic of conversation over the last four months or so, but very loosely in the background" and he had no hesitation in agreeing.

Norris says his loyalty to McLaren is based on the relationships he has within the team - starting with chief executive officer Zak Brown and team principal Andrea Stella - and their shared history.

After Norris made his F1 debut in 2019, they spent several years struggling for competitiveness, before their form turned around quickly after Stella was promoted at the end of 2022.

The team won consecutive constructors' championships in 2024 and 2025 - ending a drought that went back to 1998 - and the drivers' title for Norris last year.

The 26-year-old said: "The fact I stuck it through with them and then we went on to obviously have success certainly makes me feel like I don't want to... they didn't give up on me and I didn't give up on them.

"That just creates a very strong bond between everyone that works here. I want to believe that bond stays as strong as it is now 'til I do retire in my career at Formula 1.

"I know that's a long, long way away and I don't want to think of it. But I believe we're in the best place we've ever been even with a tough start to the season. And I believe that we can fight through anything together for sure."

McLaren started this season well off the pace they had shown through 2024 and 2025 as they struggled to get on top of the new rules introduced to F1 this year.

But Norris says that only made him want to stay at the team more.

"That's exactly the situation that doesn't take me away from where I am or doesn't influence anything else," he said.

"I still have had a lot of fun and enjoy working and trying to fight through the tougher moments with the people that I do it with now. I don't want to fight through moments with anyone else.

"This beginning of the year is the perfect example of what doesn't make me turn my head the other way or anything.

"In fact, it's more the opposite. It makes me want to stick with the people that I am with because I believe we can fight back through most circumstances and all circumstances. And I enjoy the fight in some ways just as much as I enjoy the experience of being on top."

He added: "People get too hung up sometimes on saying, 'is it the right place?' I believe it is, but even if it wasn't, the fact that I can just say I'm a driver for McLaren and I race for McLaren, that makes me happy enough."

McLaren have improved their performance significantly in recent races. After a major upgrade to their car, Norris has won the past two grands prix, in Hungary and the Netherlands.

That has reduced the gap between him and Mercedes' championship leader Kimi Antonelli to 83 points with 11 races remaining - although the war in the Middle East may affect the number of races that end up being staged.

Norris said before the British Grand Prix in July that he had been frustrated at not being able to defend his title.

Now, he says: "I'm starting the fight of defending it. I'm trying to. I'm doing my best. We all are. As a team, we're doing our best. They want to allow me to fight for it and of course I just want to fight for it. So, it's a big challenge.

"It's still a big mountain to climb in terms of trying to achieve it. But for a while now, we've been very, very close to being in the position that we are now, where we can fight for wins and podiums and we can fight the people we need to fight against.

"So, I'm certainly more confident than I have been, especially the first part of the year.

"But it still just takes a lot of work and there's a lot of things we need to improve on but we're confident as a team that we can try to achieve it."

Team principal Andrea Stella said: "Lando is an exceptional driver, who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren but, above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team.

"Since joining McLaren as part of our junior programme, he has grown with us and played a central role in bringing the team back to the front of Formula 1.

"This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together.

"With him and Oscar [Piastri, Norris' team-mate], we know we can count not only on one of the strongest partnerships but also on one of the most united and close-knit teams in Formula 1."

Zak Brown, chief executive officer of McLaren Racing, said: "Lando's journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves."

title: What will Jackson bring to Villa with Watkins set for exit?
description: BBC Sport examines what new striker Nicolas Jackson will bring to Aston Villa, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Al-Hilal.
fullText:
Aston Villa have completed the signing of Nicolas Jackson in a deal worth up to £65m, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.

Unai Emery's Villa are undergoing a major overhaul this summer, with key players including Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne having already departed.

Jackson, 25, joins a number of new additions including Johan Manzambi, Joao Gomes, Zion Suzuki and Matteo Ruggeri.

That level of squad disruption was evident on the opening weekend, when Emery's side slumped to a 4-0 defeat at Brighton.

With Watkins, 30, unavailable and both Tammy Abraham and 17-year-old Brian Madjo injured, Villa started without a recognised centre-forward - Emiliano Buendia led the line.

The arrival of Jackson - who overtakes Manzambi to become Villa's record signing - from Chelsea gives Emery a specialist striker to work with.

It also looks set to coincide with the end of Watkins' six-year spell at Villa, during which he scored 108 goals in 278 games and became one of the defining players of the rise under Emery.

However, the stats suggest Jackson is not just a like-for-like replacement for the England international - he is a different type of number nine.

On the surface, Jackson's numbers at Bayern Munich last season compare favourably with those of Watkins at Villa.

The Senegal forward scored 11 goals and provided three assists in 1,320 minutes across all competitions, averaging 1.0 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Watkins recorded 21 goals and five assists in 3,837 minutes, an average of 0.6 per 90.

Jackson also generated more attacking opportunities. He averaged 3.8 shots per 90 compared with Watkins' 2.6, and 2.2 shots on target to 1.2.

His expected-goals (xG) figure was also higher, at 0.7 per 90 compared with 0.5, while he averaged 8.5 touches in the opposition box to Watkins' 5.6.

That fits a pattern which predates his spell in Germany. Among players with at least 5,000 Premier League minutes since January 2020, only Erling Haaland has registered a higher non-penalty xG figure per 90 than Jackson's 0.55.

Getting into scoring positions has rarely been Jackson's main problem - it is his ability to finish chances which has attracted scrutiny.

During his two Premier League seasons with Chelsea, he scored 14 goals from 18.7 xG in 2023-24 and 10 from 12.3 xG the following campaign.

Jackson has converted 18 of 61 big chances in England so far, although Watkins has also missed plenty of high-value opportunities (scoring 24 of 73 since joining Villa in 2020).

Interestingly, last season's numbers suggest the gap between them was negligible. Jackson converted 19.6% of his shots and 40.9% of his big chances, compared with 18.9% and 43.2% respectively for Watkins.

There is, however, an important caveat.

Watkins started 43 matches and played almost three times as many minutes. Jackson started only 15 of his 34 appearances, and Opta says his relatively limited, substitute-heavy sample could make some of his per-90 figures look stronger than they might over a full season.

Both players were predominantly used as centre-forwards last season, making the comparison reasonably fair.

Watkins played 100% of his 3,837 minutes as a striker, with 92% coming as the central striker in Villa's 4-2-3-1.

Jackson spent 95% of his 1,320 minutes up front, with the remaining 5% on the left. At Bayern, 86% of his playing time came as the striker in a 4-2-3-1.

The similarity largely ends there. Jackson averaged 46.6 open-play touches per 90, compared with Watkins' 29.5, and completed almost twice as many passes - 24 per 90 to Watkins' 11.6.

He was also considerably more involved in creating and progressing attacks. Jackson averaged:

1.6 shot-ending carries per 90, compared with Watkins' 0.8

1.6 successful take-ons per 90, compared with 0.82

2.5 passes into the penalty area per 90, compared with 0.7.

Opta's touch maps reinforce the difference. Watkins' involvement was concentrated more heavily around the centre of the final third and penalty area, while Jackson received possession across a wider range of attacking zones.

Among a sample of 1,577 top-five European league strikers over the past 10 seasons, Jackson ranked in the 85th percentile for chances created, 77th for progressive carries and 73rd for touches.

Watkins ranked in the 28th, 53rd and eighth percentiles respectively. That points towards Villa moving from a relatively low-touch focal point to a forward who is more comfortable becoming involved in attacks earlier.

There is another possible difference when Villa lose possession. Jackson averaged 34 high pressures per 90, slightly above Watkins' 31.4, but the distinction becomes clearer in where possession was recovered.

Jackson won the ball 2.7 times per 90, compared with Watkins' 1.8, and regained it in the final third 0.9 times per 90 to Watkins' 0.6.

His percentile for possession won in the attacking third was 88th among the Opta striker sample, compared with Watkins' 43rd.

The two were almost identical for runs in behind, Jackson averaging 13 per 90 and Watkins 12.7, although the Englishman made slightly more runs which finished inside the penalty area.

Watkins also offered more aerially, winning 1.2 aerial duels per 90 compared with Jackson's 0.7, and carried the ball more directly towards goal. So Jackson would not necessarily reproduce every aspect of the player he is replacing.

Villa's interest also comes with an element of familiarity. Emery worked with Jackson at Villarreal, where the forward made 27 appearances under him, scoring three goals and providing three assists in 1,195 minutes.

Jackson has subsequently credited Emery with transforming his understanding of the game.

"Unai taught me everything about football," he said,

Jackson has explained that, when he arrived from Senegal, he possessed natural dribbling ability but had much less understanding of how and when to move.

Emery helped turn that instinctive talent into a more structured game.

Jackson's development accelerated after Emery left Villarreal. During the 2022-23 La Liga season he produced 0.56 non-penalty xG plus xA per 90, a rate bettered by only seven players with at least 1,500 minutes, all representing Barcelona, Real Madrid or Atletico Madrid.

Jackson's ability to carry the ball was already evident too. Ten of his league goal involvements followed carries, fewer only than Vinicius Jr, despite Jackson playing substantially fewer minutes.

Chelsea subsequently signed him in 2023. He scored 30 goals and supplied 12 assists in 81 appearances for the club before spending last season on loan at Bayern.

His time in Munich was complicated by circumstances rather than simply performance.

Bayern's obligation to buy would have been triggered if he reached a demanding appearance threshold, but Harry Kane remained fit and prolific, while the displays of Luis Diaz and Michael Olise limited opportunities elsewhere across the frontline.

Jackson still produced 11 goals across all competitions, and only Kane recorded a better rate of open-play Bundesliga goals per 90.

Bayern coach Vincent Kompany publicly defended him when criticism resurfaced, pointing to the quality of the forwards ahead of him and saying Jackson had trained and performed well.

Watkins has provided Villa with reliability, running power and goals throughout one of the club's most successful periods of the modern era.

Jackson arrives with a different profile. He is five years younger, gets more touches, carries the ball more frequently, creates more for others and, in limited minutes last season, generated shots and high-quality chances at an impressive rate.

There remain questions around whether those per-90 numbers would survive a heavier workload, while his finishing record at Chelsea explains why doubts have followed him.

But Villa are not buying an unknown quantity. Emery has coached Jackson before, knows the qualities he wants to develop and would be replacing a 30-year-old striker with a 25-year-old whose underlying numbers suggest there may still be considerable room to improve.

If Jackson joins and Watkins does depart, the Europa League winners will be doing more than just changing their centre-forwards.

They will be changing the way their number nine plays.

title: More British athletes convicted in connection with Baptiste case
description: BBC Sport reveals that Will Sharman, Richard Sharman and Lamin Deen were also convicted in the case which led to Leon Baptiste's imprisonment.
fullText:
Three British former athletes were convicted in Morocco as part of an investigation into the sexual assault of a minor by a sprinting coach, BBC Sport can reveal.

The prosecutions led to the imprisonment of Leon Baptiste, a UK Athletics coach and 2010 Commonwealth Games gold medallist for England in the 200m.

Baptiste was originally reported as missing in Morocco in some media articles published on 14 August, before a BBC Sport investigation revealed his conviction and jailing.

Now, court rulings seen by BBC Sport shed more light on other convictions relating to the same case.

Two-time Commonwealth silver medallist hurdler Will Sharman, his brother and ex-bobsleigh athlete Richard Sharman, and fellow former bobsleigh competitor Lamin Deen, who were all on holiday with Baptiste, were convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

Also convicted of the same offence were acquaintances Ashley O'Leary Jones and David Tuck.

The group said via their lawyers that they were never arrested and were unaware of their convictions until informed of them by BBC Sport.

A spokesperson for all five men told BBC Sport: "William, Richard, Lamin, David and Ashley are shocked and distressed by the circumstances in which they have unexpectedly found themselves.

"They reject any suggestion that they knowingly engaged in unlawful or improper conduct. They left Morocco believing they had complied with all requirements placed upon them.

"At the time, they understood that they had paid an administrative fine equivalent to approximately £40 and that the matter had concluded."

BBC Sport understands that police raided a villa in Tamensourt on the outskirts of Marrakech after a girl contacted them claiming she had been brought to the property, had not been paid money she was promised in exchange for sex with Baptiste, and that she had been assaulted by a housekeeper after she was accused of stealing a watch.

Baptiste, 41, was subsequently convicted of sexual assault of a minor and given a 10-month prison sentence, which was subsequently reduced to eight months on appeal.

Court documents refer to the girl as being 16 years old and say she suffered "psychological trauma, sexual exploitation, physical assault and injury, and the violation of her human dignity".

Court records show that in June the five men were given suspended sentences of four months and fines of 500 dirhams (£40) each after being convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

All five men were acquitted of a separate charge of inciting a minor to engage in prostitution.

The Morocco presidency of the public ministry, which oversees prosecutions in the country, provided BBC Sport with the court judgement regarding the group, which reads: "The defendants were in the company of [Leon Baptiste] and were seated at the same table as the minor, alongside her.

"They thereby assisted him in deceiving the minor and persuading her to engage in sexual relations [with Baptiste]. This constitutes participation in the enticement of a minor.

"The court found them guilty on this count and decided to convict them for these acts."

The group had already left Morocco by the time the decision was handed down. Their convictions and sentences were upheld after an appeal hearing in July.

In a response provided by their lawyers to BBC Sport, the Sharman brothers, Deen, O’Leary Jones and Tuck say they visited the Montecristo nightclub based on a recommendation provided by their driver, and had no reason to believe it was anything other than a respectable establishment.

They say they were unaware of the girl's age and that some members of the group do not even recall seeing her in the nightclub. The villa they were staying in was vast and the interaction between the men and Mr Baptiste while inside the villa was limited.

They also say that they were not present in court on any occasion, that the court process was not in English and that it was not explained to them.

The spokesperson continued: "What has unfolded over recent months has been a distressing and incoherent saga.

"They did not properly understand the proceedings and were completely shocked on being told that they were the subject of a criminal conviction, when that is not how they understood it."

Companies House records and a biography on one of O'Leary Jones' social media profiles show he is a director of a company operating five children's care homes in Greater Manchester.

Tuck's social media biography indicates he is a military veteran, while a CV posted online lists experience coaching women's and children's football clubs including at Stoke City, Apollon Limassol in Cyprus, and Orlando Pride in the USA.

When asked by BBC Sport to comment on the convictions and the potential safeguarding issues raised, the UK Foreign Office, Home Office, and Department for Culture, Media, and Sport declined to provide a response.

Records also show that other people were convicted in relation to the case.

They include the housekeeper of the villa and two of its security guards, who were each given a two-month suspended prison sentence and a fine of 5,000 dirhams (£396).

The manager of the Montecristo nightclub where the group met the girl was sentenced to two months in jail.

A waiter at the Montecristo was also prosecuted, as was the owner of the agency which rents out the villa.

The girl - a Moroccan national - was awarded civil compensation of 60,000 dirhams (£4,784), to be paid jointly by all of those convicted, plus court costs.

Baptiste is currently serving his sentence in Al-Oudaya prison, and resigned from his position as a consultant coach via a message sent on his behalf to UK Athletics on 18 August citing unspecified ill-health.

Baptiste will be deported from Morocco once he is released from prison.

His case was able to move through the system quickly, with only weeks between his initial arrest and sentencing, because Morocco operates a system in which Baptiste swiftly appeared before a judge and not a jury.

At an appeal hearing in July, two months were taken off his sentence.

The sprinters coached by Baptiste were unaware of the reason for his abrupt lack of contact since telling them he would be absent from training "for a while" in May.

Will Sharman won silver medals in the 110m hurdles at the Commonwealth Games in 2010 and 2014, as well as at the 2014 European Championships, and has worked on the BBC gameshow Gladiators.

The 41-year-old was also featured on BBC Radio 4 as an accomplished pianist in 2015, and appeared as a panel guest on an episode of A Question of Sport in 2014.

His brother Richard, 44, formerly competed in elite-level bobsleigh competitions for Great Britain. On social media he describes himself as an industrial engineer running his own company, as well as a pilot and investor.

Lamin Deen, 45, is a former lance sergeant who served in the grenadier guards during conflicts in Northern Ireland, Bosnia and Kosovo, and competed in bobsleigh at the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi and the 2018 edition in Pyeongchang.

He worked as a pundit for TNT Sports during the 2026 Games in Milan-Cortina.

In some online reviews and social media posts, the Montecristo is referred to as a known meeting place for sex workers and potential clients.

The venue was closed by Moroccan authorities during the investigation and has not reopened since.

A statement referring to the case was posted on its social media channels on 15 May, saying: "Montecristo would like to provide clarification and reaffirm its commitment to the values that have always defined us.

"We are treating this matter with the utmost seriousness and are fully co-operating with the relevant authorities in a spirit of transparency and responsibility."

BBC Sport has contacted Montecristo for comment but received no reply.

On Saturday the Moroccan charity Touche Pas À Mon Enfant (Don't Touch My Child) released a statement criticising the sentence Baptiste was given.

"While fully respecting judicial independence and the decisions handed down by competent courts, we cannot hide our astonishment and deep concern regarding a sentence of such duration in a case involving the sexual assault of a minor - particularly given that the sentence was reduced on appeal," the statement reads.

"Sexual assaults committed against children are not ordinary offences - they can leave victims with profound and lasting physical and psychological trauma.

"In this context, we question the precise legal classification of the acts and the circumstances that led to the imposition of this sentence and its subsequent reduction on appeal."

In 2016 UNAIDS estimated that around 75,000 sex workers were operating in Morocco.

The children's rights organisation Humanium has called sex tourism "a thriving industry" in Morocco.
